pr_body:
Linux kernel v4.18 (2018-08-12) added user-namespace support to FUSE, and bumped the FUSE version to 7.27 (see: torvalds/linux@da315f6e0398 (Merge tag 'fuse-update-4.18' of
git://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/mszeredi/fuse, Linus Torvalds, 2018-06-07).  This means that on such kernels it is safe to enable FUSE in nspawn containers.

In copy_devnodes(), sniff the FUSE version and if the version is >= 7.27 then copy in /dev/fuse.  We sniff the FUSE version instead of the kernel version in order to enable FUSE support on older-versioned kernels that may have the mentioned patchset backported ([as requested by @poettering][1]).  However, I am not sure that this is safe; user-namespace support is not a documented part of the FUSE protocol, which is what FUSE_KERNEL_VERSION/FUSE_KERNEL_MINOR_VERSION are meant to capture.  While the same patchset
 - added FUSE_ABORT_ERROR (which is all that the 7.27 version bump is documented as including),
 - bumped FUSE_KERNEL_MINOR_VERSION from 26 to 27, and
 - added user-namespace support

these 3 things are not inseparable; it is conceivable to me that a backport could include the first 2 of those things and exclude the 3rd; perhaps it would be safer to check the kernel version.

In append_machine_properties(), unconditionally include `"/dev/fuse", "rw"` (not "rwm") in the DeviceAllow list.  I am less familiar with now DevicePolicy/DeviceAllow work than I am with the rest of nspawn's policy stuff; I would appreciate confirmation from a reviewer that this is safe whether or not copy_devnodes() copied in /dev/fuse.

For testing, simply check that /dev/fuse can be opened for reading and writing, but that actually reading from it fails with EPERM.  The test assumes that the testsuite is running on a kernel with FUSE >= 7.27; I am unsure how to go about writing a test that validates that the version check disables FUSE on old kernels.

[1]: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/17607#issuecomment-745418835

Closes #17607

Thanks so much for fixing this! I'm the original (2020) bug reporter but have not contributed to the PR at all. My two cents:

That feels like a lot of code, complexity as well as a slight risk as the author originally mentioned, to support kernels < 4.18, i.e. more than 6 years old at this point (v4.17 = June 2018)

I don't really understand who is the target audience here. Who is going to run systemd 257, in 2025, with Linux <= 4.17 released in 2018? Who would expect this to function?

4.19 is the oldest LTS kernel today, and even that has an EOL of December 2024. My recommendation, as mentioned in #17607, is to bump `KERNEL_BASELINE_VERSION` to 4.19, and perhaps even to something newer in 2025 once 4.19 LTS EOLs. This PR then becomes far simpler: it can just assume this feature exists, i.e. no fuse version checks or kernel version checks whatsoever.

Our minimum and recommended baseline for kernels are documented in README. 

Whenever we raised the baseline people came out of the woodworks and complained. I am pretty sure we should raise it though, if we have a good reason but I am pretty sure that fuse support in nspawn doesn't quite qualify yet as reason to bump the baseline for the whole project.

We are planning to get rid of cgroupv1 support soon, and at that point we'll bump the baseline.

> Whenever we raised the baseline people came out of the woodworks and complained. I am pretty sure we should raise it though, if we have a good reason but I am pretty sure that fuse support in nspawn doesn't quite qualify yet as reason to bump the baseline for the whole project.

Agreed, that's not a good reason by itself!

That's why my argument was grounded on something objective: upstream Linux long-term support status, as documented on kernel.org. If upstream Linux doesn't support 4.17 or 4.18 for that matter, I don't see why systemd should, and I personally would think that's a pretty solid argument against anyone who complains!

And alternatively: if folks are comfortable maintaining their own fork of Linux without the help of upstream Linux, then surely they are capable with dealing with whatever incompatibilities (much newer) versions of systemd introduce, no?

But I may entirely be missing use cases or classes of users as I'm very far from the problem at hand and/or these users.

> We are planning to get rid of cgroupv1 support soon, and at that point we'll bump the baseline.

That's good to know!

> But I may entirely be missing use cases or classes of users as I'm very far from the problem at hand and/or these users.

The only thing that comes to mind regarding old kernels with new distros are embedded CPUs and SOCs where the CPU/SOC manufacturer only releases one kernel with accompanying driver blobs and that's it. There's almost no way to get a newer kernel for those, even with shims.

issue_context.title: Allow fuse in systemd-nspawn containers
issue_context.body:
@poettering, in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/2178#issuecomment-165753697 (Dec 2015) wrote:
> fuse is currently not supported in nspawn containers, because the kernel interfaces aren't compatible with namespaces/containers. Or at least they weren't the last time I looked, and leaked information from inside the container to the host. If that changed now we can certainly open that up, too.

and in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/7669#issuecomment-352388204 (Dec 2017) also wrote:
> Well, I'd love to just make fuse available by default, but iirc fuse is still not properly set up for usage in containers, i.e. just making the fuse node available is not safe, as it leaks access on host-side mounts or so, I don't remember the details about that.
> 
> If that changes we should just make FUSE available by default. Until then: you can hack around this already if you are willing to ignore the security implications around this. Just use "--bind=/dev/fuse" on the nspawn cmdline, it knows how to deal with device nodes these days.

Evidently, this has actually changed :) Linux https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/da315f6e03988a7127680bbc26e1028991b899b8 (v4.18-rc1); excerpt from the commit message:
> "The most interesting part of this update is user namespace support, mostly done by Eric Biederman. This enables safe unprivileged fuse mounts within a user namespace.

Given `@mount` is already part of the seccomp allow list for nspawn, and even `/sys/fs/fuse/` is exposed, I _think_ that, effectively, this should do it (completely untested):
```diff
diff --git a/src/nspawn/nspawn.c b/src/nspawn/nspawn.c
index 0842731c18..20e34ab9a6 100644
--- a/src/nspawn/nspawn.c
+++ b/src/nspawn/nspawn.c
@@ -2122,6 +2122,7 @@ static int copy_devnodes(const char *dest) {
                 "random\0"
                 "urandom\0"
                 "tty\0"
+                "fuse\0"
                 "net/tun\0";
 
         _cleanup_umask_ mode_t u;
```

#2178 (sshfs) and #6553 (glusterfs) have some real-world use cases. I'm interested in fuse-overlayfs (for podman) myself.

@paravoid Uhhh.... And wow does it work....

This one-line, eight-character simple patch is exactly what we needed, even without being tested. Thank you! (Well, err, I guess we just tested it)

Technically our usage case makes significant use of nspawn and we've been having difficulties with everything from filesystem binds when our usage case involves `PrivateUsers=pick`, to any type of remote filesystem. We technically wanted to use GlusterFS for our scenario, but considering it relies on FUSE, this was a significant issue. Now we're able to use GlusterFS without difficulty.

I am curious as to whether any issues (security or otherwise) will occur with this patch, but we're hopeful considering at least we have it working and no longer need to rely on unnecessarily redundant data consuming large amounts of disk space anymore.

If we come across any issues regarding this patch, I will post another comment. The only one I can think of currently would be where the userspace FUSE tools are not present on the container or host system and the device itself would be unnecessary in that case.  I do hope, however, that the systemd developers (presumably in combination with the kernel developers) inevitably decide upon a preferred solution, but, well, this should work for now in our systems! Thanks again!

> This one-line, eight-character simple patch is exactly what we needed, even without being tested. Thank you! (Well, err, I guess we just tested it)

Thank you for testing this and reporting back!

> I am curious as to whether any issues (security or otherwise) will occur with this patch, but we're hopeful considering at least we have it working and no longer need to rely on unnecessarily redundant data consuming large amounts of disk space anymore.

The most obvious one is that older kernels (for mainline that's <= 4.17), there was no namespace support for fuse, and this has no version check, which I believe would create an insecure confiugration. In another issue @poettering expressed his preference for guarding a similar feature behind a kernel feature flag, rather than a version check (to account for backports etc.), but I'm not sure what we could check here to conditionally enable this support.
If there's no sane way to check for the feature explicitly I figure we could query the fuse minor version  FUSE_KERNEL_MINOR_VERSION) from the device and base things on that.

(i.e. the point i am making, if we have to do a version check, then it should be a runtime hceck against the fuse version, and not the kernel. i.e. the more focussed and dynamic the better, since people backport features all the time to older kernels)

Anyway, happy to review/merge a patch for this.

I'm investigating how to complete this issue. Apparently it "only" needs a run-time version check on the fuse version, but I've not been able to figure out how that should be done.

   1. link and call into libfuse
   2. direct open of /dev/fuse with a FUSE_INIT check  (out.major > 7 || (out.major == 7 && out.minor >=27))
   3. some other?

Guidance please!

Any news on that? I'm having this issue while using flatpak inside an nspawn container, since flatpak nowadays uses fuse, so flatpak won't work inside nspawn.

Before anyone asks "Why use flatpak inside nspawn?" I'm building flatpaks on my homeserver and want to split off the flatpak dev environment.

FWIW, I'm not interested in this myself anymore. But as far as I know, the bug still stands.

My personal opinion is that the most reasonable path forward would be for KERNEL_BASELINE_VERSION to be higher than the current one (4.15, 6½ years old at this point), and avoid a runtime check altogether. Perhaps setting the baseline to LTS kernels would be reasonable, which would conveniently place the current minimum at 4.19 ;)

I've prepared a patch that adds the FUSE version check to `nspawn.c`, but I've discovered that @paravoid's patch no longer works with kernel 6.7.4 (I verified this with systemd c61f46fe3142e8b2fee48c845339bd82e29df085, so as to determine that it's a kernel change that broke the patch, not an nspawn change; I had to cherry-pick c29537f39e4f413a6cbfe9669fa121bdd6d8b36f and 7c5b9952c4f6e2b72f90edbe439982528b7cf223 to get it to compile).

Inside of the nspawn container, trying to use fuse results in:
```
fuse: failed to open /dev/fuse: Operation not permitted
```

Looking through the kernel commit log now to try to figure out what changed and what needs to be done differently...

> I verified this with systemd [c61f46f](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/commit/c61f46fe3142e8b2fee48c845339bd82e29df085), so as to determine that it's a kernel change that broke the patch, not an nspawn change

I should have said that I verified with *nspawn* c61f46f; I did not install an older pid1 or anything.

And as for what's different: BPF. It's `BPF_CGROUP_RUN_PROG_DEVICE_CGROUP(type, major, minor, access);` that's rejecting the `open()`.

I suspect it's the `sd_devices` BPF prog that's rejecting it, but I'll check that tomorrow.

Just gotta add `"/dev/fuse", "rw"` to the `DeviceAllow` list in `nspawn-register.c`.

Writing tests, then I'll submit a PR.

hmm logging is all over the place here. some fatal calls use LOG_WARN, some user LOG_ERR.

please clean this up.

generally, I am pretty sure we should not log beyond LOG_DEBUG if fuse is not available at all. that should not be considered an error at all. maybe just return 0 with a major/minor of zero in that case.

They all use LOG_WARN? Where are you seeing LOG_ERR?

But sure, I can demote them to LOG_DEBUG.

log_oom() uses LOG_ERR.

key is:
1. expected errors should log LOG_DEBUG at most (an expected error is that kernel might not support fuse)
2. unexpected errors should log LOG_WARNING if we ignore it and proceed
3. unexpected errors should log LOG_ERR if we fail things because of it.

Got it about `log_oom()`.

Except for `open` or the version number being too low, I don't expect any of the calls to fail. So should I use LOG_WARN for them?

yes, I agree, open() failing with some ERRNO_IS_NEG_DEVICE_ABSENT() and the version check are kinda the only "expected" failures, and hence should result in debug logging at most.

for the others LOG_WARN level would be best.

hence, my suggestion: make sure the function returns zero major/minor and >= 0 ret code in case of the two expected failures (so that they are not considered failures, but instead just "no data" success responses), with debug logging. And return negative errno failure with LOG_WARN log message for the other errors you might hit. And if everything is order, return filled in major/minor and >= 0 ret code.
This works only on relatively recent kernels, IIRC. So, `should_enable_fuse()` should handle failure here gracefully.
I'm not sure what you're asking for.

As a coding style rule when pointers are passed to functions and dereferenced without being checked for null, at the top of the receiving function assert(ptr) is added, to ensure no programming mistakes are added later during refactors and so on. You can check the rest of the code for examples
